note: Verified short quotations and excerpts from primary institutional records or original texts. Archival quotations do not imply that the speaker visited a playable scene or held office during its year. Excerpts preserve wording and case; contextual descriptions are authored summaries.

chapters.text: Education can move a nation: the future belongs to those who understand it.
chapters.author: Charles M. Vest
chapters.sourceTitle: MIT · Charles M. Vest’s inaugural address, May 10, 1991
chapters.context: Archival quotation from the Education—To Move a Nation section of Vest’s 1991 inaugural address. Presented as an archival reflection, not dialogue in the 2010, 2019 or 2024 scene.

chapters.text: The world is too interesting to ignore
chapters.author: Joseph E. Aoun
chapters.sourceTitle: Northeastern · State of the University address report, October 13, 2011
chapters.context: Archival quotation from Aoun’s discussion of expanding experiential learning beyond Boston, reported in 2011. The university’s current president biography and archives were checked in November 2026.

chapters.text: A university is the ally of change, and change is the ally of the university.
chapters.author: Gerhard Casper
chapters.sourceTitle: Stanford · Gerhard Casper’s inaugural address, October 2, 1992
chapters.context: Archival quotation from Casper’s discussion of the freedom to challenge established orthodoxy. The surrounding speech ties change to questioning assumptions and testing whether they are wrong.

chapters.text: A well-ranked university is a land of opportunity for upward mobility
chapters.author: Eric J. Barron
chapters.sourceTitle: Penn State · Remarks to the Pennsylvania Senate Appropriations Committee, February 27, 2018
chapters.context: Archival excerpt from Barron’s 2018 testimony about access and affordability. He immediately identified degree completion, especially for first-generation students, as a challenge. His presidency ended in May 2022.

chapters.text: a good part of leadership is just finding other people who can help you and do things better than you can do.
chapters.author: William H. Danforth
chapters.role: Chancellor of Washington University in St. Louis
chapters.sourceTitle: WashU Olin · William Danforth remembrance, September 16, 2020
chapters.context: Archival excerpt from Danforth’s 2018 Olin Dean’s Medal remarks, reproduced by the university in 2020. His correct university leadership title was Chancellor, not President.

chapters.text: our first priority is broadening the education experience of our students
chapters.author: Jared L. Cohon
chapters.sourceTitle: Carnegie Mellon Magazine · Speak softly, carry a giant carrot, Fall 2002
chapters.context: Archival excerpt from a 2002 university magazine account of Cohon’s meeting with Engineering and Public Policy faculty. Cohon was not president during the playable 1978 Simon chapter; this is a later archival reflection.

chapters.text: It is in times of national crisis that our true commitment to freedom of speech and thought is tested.
chapters.author: Shirley M. Tilghman
chapters.sourceTitle: Princeton · Academic Freedom and Free Expression; quotation from the September 28, 2001 inaugural address
chapters.context: Archival quotation from Tilghman’s inaugural address of September 28, 2001, reproduced verbatim on Princeton’s academic freedom page.

menu.text: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself—and you are the easiest person to fool.
menu.author: Richard P. Feynman
menu.sourceTitle: Caltech Archives · Cargo Cult Science, 1974 commencement address
menu.context: Feynman’s 1974 address on scientific integrity, preserved by Caltech’s library. The selected sentence concerns guarding against self-deception; the game does not treat a quotation as a substitute for evidence.

menu.text: ignorance more frequently begets confidence than does knowledge
menu.author: Charles Darwin
menu.sourceTitle: Darwin Online · The Descent of Man, volume I, introduction, page 3 (1871)
menu.context: Verbatim short excerpt from the original 1871 introduction, in a sentence criticizing confident declarations that a scientific problem cannot be solved. Original lower-case wording retained.
